Widow's Mite
wĭd´ōz mīt
n. phrase (the two lepta a poor widow put in the temple treasury, which the Lord weighed above all the rest)
Greek lepton, the thin one — the smallest coin in circulation; two made a kodrantes, a Roman quadrans, which Mark translates for his readers. English mite was a small Flemish copper coin, chosen by the translators as the nearest thing to nothing.

Biblical Definition

The widow's mite is observed from a seat opposite the treasury: “Jesus sat over against the treasury, and beheld how the people cast money into the treasury: and many that were rich cast in much” (Mar 12:41). “And there came a certain poor widow, and she threw in two mites, which make a farthing” (Mar 12:42). The verdict reverses the arithmetic: “this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury” (Mar 12:43), and the reason is proportion: “all they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living” (Mar 12:44). Paul states the rule: “if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not” (2Co 8:12).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines mite as a small coin, formerly current in England, a third of a farthing; and, from the Scripture, a very small quantity or particle, as of money; a small weight; and observes that the widow's mite is proverbial for a small gift from the poor.

expand to see more

MITE, n. A small weight; the twentieth part of a grain.

2. Any thing proverbially very small; a very little particle or quantity.

3. A small coin, formerly current in England, being about a third of a farthing.

The widow's mite. Mark 12.

Key Scripture

Mar 12:41 — "And Jesus sat over against the treasury, and beheld how the people cast money into the treasury: and many that were rich cast in much."

Mar 12:42 — "And there came a certain poor widow, and she threw in two mites, which make a farthing."

Mar 12:43 — "And he called unto him his disciples, and saith unto them, Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury:"

Mar 12:44 — "For all they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living."

2Co 8:12 — "For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not."

Modern Corruption

The story is used to press the poor for more, and the verse before it condemns men who devour widows' houses.

expand to see more

Mark 12:40 is the sentence immediately before the widow enters, and it is never read at the offering. The Lord has just described the scribes which devour widows' houses, and for a pretence make long prayers, and said they shall receive greater damnation. Then He sits down opposite the treasury and watches a widow put in her whole living. The two scenes are one scene. Whatever else the passage is, it is an observation of a religious system that had taught a destitute woman to give it everything she had, and the Lord's next words, in chapter 13, are that not one stone of that temple would be left upon another.

That does not cancel the commendation, and the church has rightly heard one. She gave more than all of them — the Lord says so, and the measure He uses is stated: they gave of their abundance, she of her want. The arithmetic of heaven is proportional, not absolute, which is the rule Paul lays down in 2 Corinthians 8:12 — accepted according to that a man hath. That is a comfort to the poor and a rebuke to the rich in the same clause. A large gift that cost nothing is weighed at nothing, and the widow's two coins were the heaviest thing put in that box.

The passage is also a warning about who does the weighing. Nobody in the temple court noticed the widow; the rich gave visibly and much, which is what treasuries are designed to register. Jesus sat and beheld how — not how much, but how — and called the disciples over to explain what they had missed. The doctrine of the passage is that the Lord watches giving from a seat where the amounts are visible and the proportions are what count, and that He sees the two mites go in. What a church does with that knowledge in its appeals is a matter of whether it stands with the scribes or with Him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek lepton (G3016), a mite, the thin coin; kodrantes (G2835), a farthing, quadrans; gazophulakion (G1049), the treasury; husteresis (G5304), want, poverty.

expand to see more

Greek lepta duo (G3016) — two mites; Mark 12:42, Luke 21:2; also Luke 12:59.

Greek gazophulakion (G1049) — treasury; Mark 12:41–43, Luke 21:1, John 8:20.

Greek ek tes hustereseos autes (G5304) — of her want; Mark 12:44, and Philippians 4:11 of Paul's.

Usage

"“Which devour widows' houses” — the verse before she enters."

"“Of her want did cast in all that she had” — the arithmetic is proportional."

"“Beheld how the people cast” — how, not how much."
